title: BBC Paid £130M for Lonely Planet. Why Sell at a Loss?
description:
In 1972, a young couple drove a beat-up car east from London and reached Sydney with just 27 cents left. A year later, at their kitchen table, they stapled together their first travel guide. Thirty-four years later, the buyer of their publishing company was the BBC's commercial arm.

This episode tells it in order: how a beat-up car, a misheard song and a kitchen table became Lonely Planet; how the BBC bought in twice, paying the original price for the last quarter; how Parliament called it "the worst example"; the 2013 sale, and how the "nearly £80 million" loss was worked out; and the reasons the official review finally put on record.

Where the narration cites secondary sources or estimated figures, it names the source and the method. The illustrations are AI-generated: the narrator, Ada, is a fictional character, and all other people and objects are generic cartoon figures, not real people; living people are represented only by objects. This channel has no licensing or partnership relationship with the BBC or Lonely Planet.

Information as of 2026-10-31

t001.text: You may have flipped through a thick backpacker's guidebook called Lonely Planet.

t002.text: Britain's BBC paid about 130 million pounds in total to buy the company that publishes it.

t003.text: A TV broadcaster buying a guidebook publisher is strange enough.

t004.text: But here's the surprise: six years later, the BBC sold the whole thing and got back less than half.

t005.text: And one payment in between is even stranger: the founders' last quarter, what price did the BBC pay for it?

t006.text: Plus, the BBC's own website later made a decision that even the official review called out.

t007.text: So today, let's talk about it: for 130 million pounds, what did this publisher end up bringing back?

t008.text: Our story goes back to London in 1972, and a young couple named Wheeler.

t009.text: According to a magazine interview, when the two left Britain, they had about 400 pounds between them.

t010.text: They bought a beat-up car and decided to drive east, as far as it would go.

t011.text: Afghanistan, India, Thailand, all the way to Australia.

t012.text: The day after Christmas 1972, they reached Sydney with just 27 cents between them.

t013.text: I'm a researcher at the Curio Files. They left with 400 pounds and hit Sydney with pocket change.

t014.text: In Sydney, people kept asking them: where did you go? How did you get there?

t015.text: So they just wrote all the answers into a book.

t016.text: In 1973, right at the kitchen table, the two of them wrote and stapled the copies one by one.

t017.text: The title meant crossing Asia on the cheap, and it was under 100 pages.

t018.text: Guess how many copies a homemade stapled book sold in its first week?

t019.text: 1,500. That's what the publisher itself says in its front pages.

t020.text: I first thought it had an extra zero.

t021.text: With books selling, the publisher needed a name. Where did it come from?

t022.text: An English song. The lyric was lovely planet.

t023.text: But Tony Wheeler kept singing it as lonely planet.

t024.text: Maureen corrected him. He later admitted: she was right, I always got the lyric wrong.

t025.text: And the misheard name just stuck.

t026.text: In 1975, they put out another book, all about Southeast Asia.

t027.text: Backpackers later gave that book a nickname. What was it?

t028.text: The nickname: the Yellow Bible. That's what a 1992 article called it.

t029.text: Tony Wheeler said wherever the books went, people followed.

t030.text: Guess how big that little kitchen-table book grew?

t031.text: By 2007, it had over 500 titles and sold more than 6.5 million copies a year.

t032.text: Its website had 4.3 million visitors a month.

t033.text: On October 1 that year, someone came knocking.

t034.text: It was the BBC's commercial arm. It bought three quarters of the company.

t035.text: The price wasn't announced then; a later BBC press release spelled it out: 88.1 million pounds.

t036.text: The remaining quarter stayed with the Wheelers.

t037.text: So what was the BBC after with all that money?

t038.text: The commercial arm's chief executive said: to grow its content brands online, and expand in Australia and the US.

t039.text: If you're British, your first thought is probably: what about my licence fee?

t040.text: The BBC later stressed no public money was used.

t041.text: Inside the BBC, a watchdog trust didn't say yes right away either.

t042.text: It wanted the BBC to prove first that this deal would make its programmes and brand worth more.

t043.text: When the news broke, The Guardian and the FT tore into it the same day.

t044.text: A Guardian editorial called it "clumsy commercialisation."

t045.text: To be fair: The Guardian noted in the piece that it's a competitor too.

t046.text: But two years later, Parliament was the one attacking.

t047.text: In April 2009, the Commons Culture, Media and Sport Committee issued a report.

t048.text: It said the balance had tipped too far toward the commercial arm's unchecked expansion.

t049.text: Worse were the books. In the year to the end of March 2009, it lost 3.2 million pounds.

t050.text: In September, the committee added another report. What word did it use this time?

t051.text: The commercial arm had moved into areas with little link to the BBC's core, and this buy was the worst example.

t052.text: The report also said the watchdog trust seemed arrogant.

t053.text: That month, a London city magazine's founder said it lost money hand over fist,

t054.text: the BBC kept pouring in millions. Why not force them to sell it?

t055.text: At year's end the Trust ruled: no more such deals, barring exceptional circumstances.

t056.text: If you were a BBC executive then, what would you do? Sell, or hang on?

t057.text: They hung on. And the business really seemed to turn around.

t058.text: In February 2011, papers reported it back in profit, earning 1.9 million pounds.

t059.text: The share of revenue from outside print rose from 9 percent to 22 percent.

t060.text: That same month, the Wheelers played a card from their contract.

t061.text: This card was a put option: the right to make the buyer take the rest.

t062.text: Remember the question from the start? What price for that last quarter?

t063.text: At the original purchase price. The BBC paid 42.17 million pounds.

t064.text: If you were the seller, that might be the best contract you ever signed.

t065.text: The official review later put it bluntly: this put option was poorly designed.

t066.text: Why? Results were clearly below forecast, yet the price wasn't discounted at all.

t067.text: The chairman at the time did defend the card:

t068.text: he said the option let the company draw on the Wheelers' experience for three and a half years.

t070.text: That's the roughly 130 million pounds from the start.

t071.text: Then, that May, Australian publishing media reported that up to 70 jobs would be cut in Melbourne,

t072.text: and much of the web work would move to London.

t073.text: And the Wheelers left the company they had built from scratch.

t074.text: But to make money online, this company couldn't rely on itself alone. Who did it rely on?

t075.text: The review said its online business was meant to plug into the BBC's international website and sell ads together.

t076.text: Remember that decision by the BBC's own website?

t077.text: First, that website was delayed; the report said this made decent ad money even harder.

t078.text: And then? Guess what it did next.

t079.text: After the delay, it decided to build its own travel section.

t080.text: Pay a fortune for a travel company, then build your own travel section? Isn't that odd?

t081.text: Like buying a coffee machine but still buying coffee downstairs daily.

t082.text: Print was shrinking too: US travel book sales in 2012 were down 19 percent from the year before.

t084.text: Last trip abroad, did you find restaurants in a book, or in reviews on your phone?

t085.text: By March 2013, the BBC had had enough.

t086.text: On March 19, the BBC announced it was selling the whole company for 75 million Australian dollars.

t088.text: At the time of sale, its website drew over 120 million visitors a year,

t089.text: and its phone apps had been downloaded more than 11 million times.

t090.text: The buyer was a company headquartered in Nashville, Tennessee,

t091.text: its main owner a Kentucky-born landowner who got rich on discount cigarettes.

t092.text: The backpacker's bible ended up with a cigarette tycoon. Who saw that coming?

t093.text: The official reason: it no longer fit the plan to put the BBC's own brands at the core.

t094.text: So how much did the BBC lose?

t095.text: At the time, AFP and The Guardian both wrote: nearly 80 million pounds.

t096.text: The math is simple: that 130 million from the start, minus the sale price.

t098.text: The money wasn't all lost on the day of the sale.

t099.text: The Guardian wrote that over six years, the BBC had already written down 67 million pounds.

t100.text: Its book value fell from that 130 million at the start all the way to 63 million.

t101.text: So on sale day, what was left to lose?

t103.text: On announcement day, the trust admitted: it was not a good commercial investment.

t104.text: And what did the people who sold to the BBC think of the deal?

t105.text: That September, AP interviewed Tony Wheeler.

t106.text: He said: no question, we sold at the perfect time.

t107.text: He said it wasn't just the economy that hurt the company; when they sold, the Australian dollar was taking off.

t108.text: He also said the BBC missed one thing: its best sales were in Italian-language guidebooks.

t109.text: Two months later, the review the trust had asked the BBC to do itself came out.

t110.text: It said the company moved too slowly online, when it might have gone the way of TripAdvisor,

t111.text: or caught the later wave of home sharing.

t112.text: The report also traced problems back to the day of purchase: the plan assumed a 30 percent operating margin.

t113.text: It called that too optimistic; the buyer seemed swept up in the deal's momentum.

t114.text: Nor did it really work out how fast print would fall.

t115.text: So is this all the BBC's own fault?

t116.text: The report also listed things beyond its control.

t117.text: First, the Australian dollar's unexpected surge. Remember Tony Wheeler on that?

t118.text: Plus the financial crisis and structural strain on bookstores.

t119.text: The report also said that over those years, the BBC put in about 20 million pounds more.

t120.text: Working from the report's own figures, with everything in, the loss comes close to 100 million pounds.

t121.text: That same month, the trust's vice-chair said mistakes were made in buying and running it.

t122.text: The story's not over. Remember that beat-up car driving east from London?

t123.text: Two years later, at a writers' festival in Bali, Tony Wheeler told Reuters even more bluntly:

t124.text: it was an absolute disaster. They bought this car, then didn't fill the tank or hit the gas.

t125.text: They got in and just asked: what do we do? Let's drive slowly, then.

t126.text: Where did it go after the BBC?

t127.text: At the end of 2020, it was sold again, for an undisclosed price.

t128.text: Today it has about 130 full-time staff; the year the BBC sold it, it had 400.

t129.text: The books are still coming out, translated into 33 languages, with over 150 million copies printed.

t130.text: Back to our question: 130 million pounds in, less than half back. Why?

t131.text: The review's answer: overvalued, too slow to change, and bad timing.

t132.text: At that kitchen table in 1973, the book was written to answer one question: how did you get there?

t133.text: Over 30 years later, the BBC bought it asking a different question: can it make the BBC brand worth more?

t134.text: For me, that's why this account is so hard to settle: those two questions were never the same.

t135.text: Do you still take a guidebook abroad, or just your phone? Tell me in the comments.

t136.text: This channel only covers what's on record. To keep digging through the files, subscribe.
